title: States vs operators

a.definition: The initial state, the intermediate states along the way, and the goal state of a problem.

b.definition: The rules that say which moves are allowed. Applying one changes the problem from one state to another.

diff: The problem space is the set of states, and operators are what connect them. Knowing the initial and goal states does not tell you which intermediate states link them, so solving means finding a sequence of operator applications that reaches the goal.
example: In the Tower of Hanoi the starting stack is the initial state and the completed stack on the target peg is the goal. The operators are one disk at a time, only a disk with nothing on top, and never a larger disk on a smaller one.
watch: Stating the goal exactly does not solve the problem. In the numbered-tile puzzle you can describe the finished board and still not know the moves.

title: Problem solving as search vs as restructuring

a.definition: Problem solving as the activity between posing a problem and reaching its solution, finding a route through possible states. Means-end analysis reduces the difference between the current state and the goal.

b.definition: A perceptual view in which the way the problem is organized in the mind affects which solution is available. Restructuring reorganizes the representation so a hidden relationship becomes usable.

diff: Search is about moving through states step by step. Restructuring is about changing the representation so the answer appears. Some problems are solved by successive operations, and others by a sudden reorganization.
example: In Köhler's circle problem, the black line is one diagonal of a rectangle whose other diagonal is a radius, and the two diagonals of a rectangle are equal, so x = r.
watch: Newell and Simon developed the Logic Theorist for the search view. Do not attribute restructuring to them.

title: Insight vs noninsight problems

a.definition: Solved by a sudden realization after the representation changes, as in the triangle and chain problems.

b.definition: Solved by successive operations that bring the solver closer, as in algebra.

diff: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) had people rate warmth every 15 seconds. For algebra, warmth rose gradually as the solution approached. For insight problems it stayed low until close to the solution and then jumped sharply, from about 3 to 7. People cannot anticipate how near they are on insight problems.
example: In Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), triangle and chain problems were compared with algebra.
watch: Not every problem is solved with an Aha experience. Some allow a methodical route.

title: Functional fixedness vs mental set

a.definition: Restricting an object to its familiar function.

b.definition: A preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on past experience with that problem or similar ones.

diff: Fixedness is about an object's use, and a set is about a method of solving. Both are forms of fixation, which Gestalt psychologists saw as a major obstacle.
example: Seeing the matchbox only as a container blocks the candle solution. In the water-jug problems the familiar B − A − 2C procedure blocks the simpler A + C and A − C.
watch: Ask whether the block is about what an object is for or about which procedure keeps being applied.

title: Candle problem vs two-string problem

a.definition: Mount a candle on a corkboard so wax does not drip. The solution is to tack the matchbox to the board as a platform. Participants given empty matchboxes were twice as likely to solve it.

b.definition: Tie together two strings hanging too far apart to reach both. The solution is to tie pliers to one string as a pendulum weight. When an experimenter accidentally set a string in motion, most participants solved it.

diff: Both are functional fixedness. In the candle problem the box is seen as a container and not a platform. In the two-string problem the pliers are seen as a gripping tool and not a weight. In the two-string problem a hint that restructured the representation made the string something that could swing within reach.
example: The objects and the requirements stay the same, but the solver uses a different relationship among them.
watch: Both solutions require a new use for a familiar object.

title: Blank board vs bread-and-butter board

a.definition: The squares are unlabeled or only colored, so nothing points the solver toward the pairing a domino needs.

b.definition: The squares are labeled bread and butter, which emphasizes the difference between the two kinds of square and the pairing a domino needs.

diff: How a problem is stated changes its difficulty. The labels made it easier to represent a domino as needing one of each kind. Participants in the bread-and-butter condition solved the problem twice as fast as those with the blank board.
example: With a think-aloud protocol, solvers in the bread-and-butter condition shift from treating squares as positions to considering the relationship between the two kinds of square.
watch: The objects and the requirement did not change. Only the representation did.

title: Total area vs pairing (mutilated checkerboard)

a.definition: 62 squares matches the area of 31 dominoes, so it seems the board can be covered.

b.definition: Every domino covers one square of each color, and the two removed corners are the same color, so the colors are unequal.

diff: Equal total area does not guarantee a legal arrangement. The color imbalance applies to every possible placement, so the covering is impossible. Reasoning in terms of pairs exposes a constraint area alone hides.
example: An ordinary board has 64 squares and 32 dominoes cover it. Remove two opposite corners and 62 squares remain, but they are 30 of one color and 32 of the other, while 31 dominoes would need 31 of each.
watch: Moving the dominoes around cannot change the imbalance.

title: Goal vs subgoal

a.definition: The condition you are trying to reach, such as the whole stack moved to the third peg.

b.definition: A condition that makes part of the larger task possible, not the final answer.

diff: Means-end analysis organizes search around reducing the difference between the current situation and the goal, and subgoals are the steps that do it. Different subgoals address different obstacles to the same move, one at the source and one at the destination.
example: In the Tower of Hanoi, the first subgoal is freeing the large disk. The second is freeing the third peg. The third is moving the large disk.
watch: A subgoal is not the final answer, and the smaller disks still have to be brought over afterward.

title: Surface features vs structural features

a.definition: The specific elements used to describe a problem, such as a fortress, a tumor, a lightbulb, a laser or a ray.

b.definition: The underlying principle that governs the solution, such as a strong force that would damage the surroundings if sent through one path.

diff: Surface features are what the objects are, and structural features are why a solution works. Similar surface features can help a person notice a possible link, but transfer depends on matching structure. Two lightbulb versions can keep the same surface features while changing the structure.
example: In the radiation and fragile-glass problems a strong ray would damage the surroundings on its way to an internal target, so several low-intensity beams must converge.
watch: A fortress and a tumor do not look alike, yet they share the structure.

title: Noticing vs mapping vs applying

a.definition: Recognizing that a source problem may be relevant to the target. It is crucial and can be the hardest step.

b.definition: Linking the elements and relationships of the source to the target, then using that link to generate a parallel solution.

diff: Gick and Holyoak distinguished these steps. After reading the fortress story only about 30 percent of participants solved the radiation problem, and when told to think about the story success rose to about 75 percent. Having the source in memory did not guarantee spontaneous use, which points to noticing as a major bottleneck.
example: In the Russian marriage problem mapped to the checkerboard, marriages correspond to dominoes and the two groups of people to the two square colors.
watch: Do not describe noticing as the same thing as mapping. Noticing is finding the source.

title: Source problem vs target problem

a.definition: A problem with relevant similarities whose solution guides a new problem.

b.definition: The problem currently being solved.

diff: Analogical problem solving transfers a solution from the source to the target. The useful information is the relationship among the elements, not their identical appearance.
example: The Russian marriage problem is the source and the mutilated checkerboard is the target. Duncker's radiation problem is the source for the lightbulb problem.
watch: The target is what you need to solve now. The source is what you already know.

title: Spontaneous vs prompted use of an analogy

a.definition: A source in memory is used without a hint. After just reading the fortress story, about 30 percent of participants solved the radiation problem.

b.definition: The person is told to think about the story they read. Then about 75 percent solved the radiation problem.

diff: The people and the story in memory were the same, and only the hint differed. So having the source available was not enough: the reminder made the relevant source available for mapping and application, and noticing is a major bottleneck. Only about 10 percent reach the solution without a helpful analogy.
example: Gick and Holyoak's fortress story: a rebel general sends small groups along different roads so mines do not explode, and they arrive together to attack.
watch: Having a source in memory is not the same as using it.

title: Fragile-glass vs insufficient-intensity lightbulb sources

a.definition: A high-intensity beam would break the glass, which matches the healthy-tissue constraint. About 69 percent who read it solved the radiation problem.

b.definition: The laser can only make low-intensity beams that cannot fuse the filament, so beams are combined, but there is no surrounding-damage constraint. About 33 percent solved it.

diff: Both use converging beams, so the surface story is similar, but the structural constraint differs. The transfer rates follow how well the underlying constraint matches the target.
example: About 69 percent who read the fragile-glass version solved the radiation problem, against about 33 percent who read the insufficient-intensity version.
watch: Both are lightbulb sources. The difference is the surrounding-damage constraint.

title: Lightbulb with vs without the radiation source

a.term: With the radiation problem as a source
a.definition: The tumor and the filament are both targets needing a strong local effect, and healthy tissue and fragile glass are both surroundings that a single strong approach would damage. About 81 percent solved the lightbulb problem.

b.definition: About 10 percent solved the lightbulb problem.

diff: The radiation problem works as a source because it shares the structure, and the surface features also overlap, since both direct a beam toward an internal target, which makes the link easier to notice.
example: Ruth's sealed lightbulb has a broken filament, and several low-intensity lasers from different directions fuse it without breaking the glass.
watch: The solution is several weak beams converging, not one strong beam.

title: Experts vs novices organizing problems

a.definition: Physics professors who sorted problems by structural features, such as conservation of energy.

b.definition: Students with one semester of physics who sorted problems by surface features, such as inclined planes.

diff: In Chi et al. (1982) the same problem 24 got a different partner under the two organizations. Novices paired 23 and 24 because both have inclines, and experts paired 21 and 24 through conservation of energy even though 21 has a block and spring on a horizontal surface. Expertise changes which relationship is the basis for similarity.
example: Chi et al. (1982) had physics professors and students sort 24 physics problems into groups by similarity.
watch: Novices go by what the problem looks like. Experts go by the principle that solves it.

title: Meaningful vs random chess positions

a.definition: A master sees familiar groups of pieces and recalls each group as one chunk drawn from long-term memory.

b.definition: The same kinds of pieces on the same board with no meaningful relationships, so there are no familiar chunks and the master must remember piece by piece.

diff: Chase and Simon (1973) compared a chess master with a beginner who had fewer than 100 hours of experience, giving each five seconds with the board. The master was much better on real positions and the advantage was greatly reduced on random ones, so the edge comes from organized domain knowledge and not a general memory advantage.
example: The pieces were of the same kinds in both conditions, and only the meaning of the arrangement changed.
watch: A chess master does not have a better memory in general.

title: Comparing sources vs using one source

a.definition: Applying a single familiar story or problem to a new target, so what you notice depends on how much the target looks like that source.

b.definition: Comparing two sources and working out what they share, for example two stories in which separate weak forces converge on one target.

diff: With one source, the structure is buried in that story's details. With two sources the details do not match, so what is left in common is the structure, which directs reasoning toward structural features. A later target can then be approached through the common relationship and not through one familiar situation.
example: Compare the fortress story with a second convergence story, then try the radiation problem.
watch: Analogical encoding is about comparing sources, not about being reminded of one.

title: Laboratory analogies vs in vivo analogies

a.definition: Researchers give a source and a target under controlled conditions, and people often fail to use the analogy on their own, as when the fortress story helped only about 30 percent.

b.definition: Researchers observe people solving real problems in their ordinary setting, where analogies are used routinely.

diff: This is the analogical paradox: analogies are hard to use in the laboratory and routine in real work. In vivo research keeps the ordinary context but is time-consuming and gives up control of variables, while laboratory work isolates variables but removes the context.
example: Fortress to radiation gave about 30 percent unprompted, while scientists use about 3 to 15 analogies in a one-hour laboratory meeting.
watch: The paradox is a contrast in how often analogies are used, not a contradiction in the theory.

title: Expert strengths vs expert limits

a.definition: An expert is extremely knowledgeable after a very long time learning and practicing, perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 hours for chess. Experts solve problems in their field faster and more successfully than beginners and spend more time analyzing before proceeding.

b.term: Outside the field and in new situations
b.definition: The advantage is specific to the field, so experts are no better than novices outside it. Too much knowledge can lock in a familiar approach and make the expert less open to new ways of looking at a problem.

diff: The same knowledge causes both. It lets experts recognize the principle behind a problem, as in Chi et al. (1982), but when a problem needs the usual procedure dropped, the knowledge can act like a mental set.
example: Physics professors in Chi et al. (1982) sorted problems by principle, which is a strength. A familiar procedure dominating, as in the water-jug problems, shows the limit.
watch: Expert does not mean better at everything.

title: Triangle problem vs chain problem

a.definition: Ten dots form an upward-pointing triangle, and you must move exactly three dots to make it point down, with seven staying in place.

b.definition: Four short sections of chain must become one closed loop, where opening a link costs 2 cents, closing it costs 3 cents and the budget is 15 cents.

diff: Both are insight problems used by Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987), and both are solved by a change in representation. In the triangle the top dot becomes a new bottom point, and in the chain one three-link section is opened into separate links that join the other three sections.
example: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) compared both with algebra and found warmth jumped late for them, from about 3 to 7.
watch: In the chain problem three open-and-close operations use the full 15 cents.

title: Problem vs knowing the goal

a.definition: A situation with a present state, a goal and an obstacle between them, where the solution is not immediately obvious.

b.definition: Being able to describe exactly what the finished situation looks like.

diff: The difficulty is the route and not whether the goal has been stated. In the numbered-tile puzzle you can describe the goal arrangement exactly and still not know the sequence of moves that gets there.
example: The initial state is 8, empty, 6 over 5, 4, 7 over 2, 3, 1, and the goal is empty, 1, 2 over 3, 4, 5 over 6, 7, 8.
watch: A tile being on the board does not mean it is in its required position, because the whole arrangement defines the state.

title: Russian marriage problem vs mutilated checkerboard

a.definition: There are 32 bachelors and 32 unmarried women. After two bachelors die, 30 men and 32 women remain and the question is whether 31 heterosexual marriages can be formed. The answer is no.

b.definition: Removing two opposite corners leaves 62 squares, which matches the area of 31 dominoes, but the two removed squares are the same color so the covering is impossible.

diff: Marriages correspond to dominoes, the two groups of people correspond to the two square colors, and removing two bachelors corresponds to removing two same-colored squares. The useful information transferred from the source is the relationship among the elements and not their identical appearance.
example: A valid marriage needs one member of each group, just as a domino needs one square of each color.
watch: Dividing 62 by two gives 31 pairs by total size but ignores which kinds each pair must contain.

title: Having an idea vs creative problem solving

a.definition: Generating a novel idea or new connection. Divergent thinking is open-ended and allows many potential solutions.

b.definition: A fuller process that includes problem generation, formulation, solving with evaluation and planning, and solution implementation, usually after a lengthy period of trial and error.

diff: Ideas are necessary, since without them the process stops, but generating them does not evaluate, plan or carry out a response.
example: Finding the problem, defining it and finding ideas come before evaluating and acting on them.
watch: Creativity is more than getting an idea.
